case.label: C
case.text: A candidate who remembers that SSE-KMS involves data keys might argue GenerateDataKey is the KMS action S3 needs on the key; but the stem says the application only downloads existing objects, and downloads need only kms:Decrypt, so the case fails. The 'only downloads' sentence is the deciding constraint and is stated explicitly; no second answer survives. Twin of kms-q006 (upload variant), options are parallel, no wording cue beyond the action names.

case.label: B
case.text: Calling Encrypt directly with the KMS key does keep the key under security-team control and lets other authorized principals decrypt; it fails only because Encrypt accepts a small plaintext (a few KB), and the stem rules it out with 'large video files' and 'encrypt each file itself'. A and D differ by one word (plaintext vs encrypted data key), which a careful reader resolves at once; the pair slightly cues that one of the two is the key, but not which.

case.label: C
case.text: A KMS key in a CloudHSM key store is still a customer managed key with a key policy the team writes, and its use is logged in CloudTrail, so it meets both functional requirements; it loses only on 'LEAST operational overhead' because the company must run a CloudHSM cluster. A fails because AWS managed key policies cannot be edited; D fails because AWS owned keys are not visible or controllable in the account. The overhead qualifier decides cleanly.

case.label: A
case.text: A also gives the role the IAM-side permission and, combined with C, would let decryption succeed; it loses only to B on least privilege because of the wildcard resource. Side note, not a second answer: reading the objects from the S3 bucket in account A would also need a bucket policy, which no option offers; the stem frames the need as decrypting under the key, so this gap does not change the key. D fails because an SCP never grants permissions.

case.label: C
case.text: A candidate who knows that SSE-KMS uploads sometimes need kms:Decrypt (multipart uploads, which must decrypt data keys to assemble parts) could pick Decrypt; the stem closes this by saying single PUT requests, where only kms:GenerateDataKey is required. The deciding constraint is explicit. Twin of kms-q001.

case.label: B
case.text: KMS keys in the default key store are generated and kept in FIPS-validated HSMs, are available across AZs, and need the least operations, so a candidate who reads 'HSM' loosely could pick B; but the stem demands single-tenant HSMs under the company's exclusive control and an unchanged JCE interface, which KMS (multi-tenant, AWS-operated, KMS API) does not give. C meets single-tenancy but is not on AWS and adds heavy overhead. Decisive constraints are explicit.

case.label: A
case.text: Grants do let the developer roles call Decrypt without IAM policies, so A fixes today's failures; it fails the second requirement (manage access centrally with IAM policies) and adds per-role overhead. B and D fail because no IAM policy works while the key policy lacks the account-principal statement. The 'centrally manage with IAM policies' sentence decides; no second answer.

case.label: B
case.text: The AWS managed key for S3 does rotate its key material yearly with zero work, so B meets the rotation rule with low overhead; it fails because the security team would lose control of the key policy (AWS managed key policies cannot be changed). C works but with large re-encryption overhead. The 'keep control of the key policy' sentence decides; no second answer.

case.label: B
case.text: B looks like the lower-overhead path because it avoids re-encryption, and a candidate who does not know that a single-Region key cannot be converted to a multi-Region key would pair B with A; but the conversion is not possible, so B fails. Minor note on A: a replica created with the default key policy would let an IAM policy grant access instead, so A is one valid way rather than the only way, but it is the only option among the five that gives the role access to the replica. Mild cue: A presupposes a 'replica key', pointing to B or D. E leaves a gap of not-yet-re-encrypted data during an outage and adds a recurring job.

case.label: D
case.text: An explicit deny in the key policy for all cryptographic operations also stops every use at once and is reversible by removing the statement (PutKeyPolicy is not a cryptographic operation), so D meets the functional requirements; it loses on overhead and risk of a policy-editing error compared with one Disable call. B fails because the longest deletion waiting period (30 days) is shorter than the 60-day legal review. C fails because the key policy and grants could still allow use. The LEAST overhead qualifier decides.

case.label: D
case.text: On-demand rotation keeps the key ID and alias and needs no code change, so D would be ideal if it applied; it does not, because on-demand and automatic rotation support only symmetric encryption keys, and A fails because key material cannot be imported into a key whose origin is AWS_KMS (and a key never takes different key material). Wording cue: the stem stresses 'through an alias, not through its key ID', and B is the only option that changes the alias, which hints at manual rotation. Customers also need the new public key, but that is not a code change to the signing applications.

case.label: A
case.text: A candidate with older study material (KMS HSMs once validated at FIPS 140-2 Level 2) would believe only CloudHSM reaches Level 3 and pick A; current AWS KMS documentation states KMS keys are protected by FIPS 140-3 Security Level 3 validated HSMs, so C meets the requirement while keeping the KMS SDK calls and key policies. A also breaks the existing KMS SDK calls and has no key policy. The item tests the recent change; it is not ambiguous on current facts, but it may read as a trap for readers using pre-change prep material.
